title: Macfarlane's Witchcraft in Tudor and Stuart England: First Quantitative Regional Study
description: Alan Macfarlane published Witchcraft in Tudor and Stuart England: A Regional and Comparative Study in 1970, a landmark work that applied quantitative social-historical methods to Essex witchcraft records, analyzing 500 cases over 160 years. Macfarlane independently arrived at the same charity-refusal model as Keith Thomas (whose book appeared the following year), demonstrating its empirical basis in actual accusation patterns. His analysis showed that accused and accusers typically knew each other, that accusations followed neighbor disputes, and that the accused were disproportionately old women — findings that have been replicated across other English regions. Macfarlane also applied anthropological frameworks from Max Marwick's study of Central African witchcraft to understand the social function of witch accusation in communities undergoing the transition from communal to more individualistic economic relations.
historiographical_note: Macfarlane's quantitative approach and use of anthropological theory represented a methodological innovation that influenced subsequent regional studies. His thesis about the relation between witch accusation and the breakdown of traditional communal charity was refined by James Sharpe and challenged by Robin Briggs (for France), who found different accusation patterns. The Essex findings remain solid even where the theoretical framework has been questioned.
source_method: Macfarlane, Witchcraft in Tudor and Stuart England (1970); Essex assize records; subsequent scholarship engaging with Macfarlane
